front: A ball is tossed straight up from a cart rolling at constant velocity. Where does it land?
why: Ball tossed from a moving cart lands in the hand; classic independence-of-components question

front: A ball thrown upward returns to its launch height with speed:
why: Symmetric vertical throw returns at equal speed; commonly tested free-fall fact

front: A boat aims straight across a flowing river. What sets its crossing time and landing point?
why: River crossing time set only by the perpendicular component is a common vector problem

front: A bullet fired horizontally and one dropped from the same height: which lands first?
why: Fired vs dropped bullet landing together is the classic test of independent components

front: A long jumper leaves the ground at 8 m/s and 30 degrees. Estimate the jump distance.
why: Range calculation applied to a long jump; worked example of the range formula

front: A person falls 2 m onto the floor. Estimate impact speed and fall time using $g = 10$.
why: v = sqrt(2gh) and t = v/g estimate is a commonly used free-fall calculation

front: A projectile is launched at 30° above the horizontal at 20 m/s. What is the horizontal component of its initial velocity?
why: Resolving v0 cos(theta) is a calculation done on essentially every exam

front: A runner completes a 400 m lap in 50 s. Compare average speed with average velocity.
why: Average speed vs average velocity on a closed lap is a common discrete

front: A skydiver at terminal velocity opens a parachute. Describe the motion that follows.
why: Parachute opening reverses acceleration direction; plausible but secondary scenario

front: A sprinter's v-t curve rises steeply and then flattens at 11 m/s. Where is acceleration greatest, and what does the plateau mean?
why: Reading acceleration off a sprinter's v-t curve; graph reading is covered by higher cards

front: A stone dropped from a cliff hits water after 3 s ($g=10$). Cliff height?
why: d = 1/2 g t^2 free-fall calculation appears on essentially every exam

front: A velocity-time graph crosses zero and changes sign. What is physically happening?
why: v-t graph crossing zero means reversal; commonly tested graph interpretation

front: Air resistance causes a falling object to:
why: Air resistance leading to terminal velocity; the definition card is higher, this restates it

front: An elevator moving upward begins to slow. What is the direction of its acceleration?
why: Slowing elevator has acceleration opposite motion; common conceptual question

front: An object dropped from rest covers what distances in successive equal time intervals?
why: The 1:3:5:7 ratio is a neat consequence of t^2 scaling but rarely the tested point

front: An object has negative velocity and positive acceleration. Describe its motion.
why: Negative velocity with positive acceleration means slowing; common sign-reasoning question

front: Area under a velocity-time graph gives {{c1::displacement}}; area under an acceleration-time graph gives {{c1::change in velocity}}.
why: Area under v-t is displacement, under a-t is change in velocity; tested every year

front: At 30 m/s, roughly how far does a car travel during a 0.7 s reaction time?
why: Reaction-distance numeric example is illustrative, not outline content

front: At the top of a vertical throw, velocity is {{c1::zero}} but acceleration is {{c1::still g downward}}.
why: Zero velocity but acceleration g at the apex is tested on nearly every exam

front: Average velocity is {{c1::displacement over time}}, and equals $(v_0 + v)/2$ only if {{c1::acceleration is constant}}.
why: Average velocity as displacement/time and the constant-acceleration shortcut are foundational

front: Deceleration means {{c1::speed is decreasing}}, which requires acceleration to {{c1::oppose velocity}}, not merely to be negative.
why: Deceleration means acceleration opposes velocity, not merely negative; common sign question

front: Displacement is a {{c1::vector}} while distance is a {{c1::scalar}}, so a round trip has zero displacement.
why: Vector displacement vs scalar distance is a foundational distinction tested every year

front: Doubling launch speed at fixed angle multiplies range by {{c1::4}} and maximum height by {{c1::4}}.
why: Range and height scale with v0^2; commonly tested proportional reasoning

front: Doubling the height of a free fall changes impact speed by a factor of:
why: Impact speed scales with sqrt(h); commonly tested proportionality

front: For a distance formula, $at^2$ carries units of {{c1::meters}}, while $vt^2$ carries {{c1::meters times seconds}} and cannot be a distance.
why: Unit-checking at^2 vs vt^2 is generic dimensional advice

front: For a symmetric projectile flight, time up equals {{c1::time down}} and landing speed equals {{c1::launch speed}}.
why: Time up equals time down and speed symmetry are commonly tested projectile facts

front: For projectiles, horizontal velocity is {{c1::constant}}, and vertical acceleration is {{c2::-g (downward)}}.
why: Constant horizontal velocity with vertical acceleration -g is the core projectile model

front: From a velocity-time graph, how do you find position at a later time?
why: Finding position from a v-t graph restates the area-under-curve card

front: How do you choose which Big 5 kinematic equation to use?
why: Choosing a Big 5 equation by the missing variable is strategy supporting the equations card

front: How do you get a projectile's maximum height without first finding time?
why: h = v0y^2/(2g) for max height is a commonly used calculation shortcut

front: How does acceleration evolve during a fall with air resistance?
why: Acceleration decaying to zero during a fall with drag; secondary graph-shape detail

front: How does launch angle change range at a fixed launch speed?
why: 45 degrees maximizing range restates the range-formula card in this deck

front: How should you estimate free-fall numbers quickly on the exam?
why: Using g = 10 for quick free-fall numbers is useful estimation advice

front: In free fall the a-t graph is a horizontal line, so the v-t graph is {{c1::a straight line}} and the x-t graph is {{c1::a parabola}}.
why: Constant a gives linear v-t and parabolic x-t; commonly tested graph shapes

front: Launch components: horizontal is {{c1::$v_0\cos\theta$}} and vertical is {{c1::$v_0\sin\theta$}}.
why: Launch components v0 cos and v0 sin are used in calculations every year

front: On a frictionless incline, acceleration along the surface is {{c1::$g\sin\theta$}}.
why: Acceleration g sin(theta) on a frictionless incline is a calculation used on essentially every exam

front: On a position-time graph the slope is {{c1::velocity}}; on a velocity-time graph the slope is {{c1::acceleration}}.
why: Slope of x-t is velocity and slope of v-t is acceleration; tested every year

front: On a position-time graph, concave up means {{c1::positive acceleration}} while any straight line means {{c1::zero acceleration}}.
why: Concavity on an x-t graph signals acceleration sign; commonly tested graph reading

front: On a velocity-time graph, area below the axis counts as {{c1::negative displacement}}, so total distance needs {{c1::areas added as magnitudes}}.
why: Signed area below the axis vs total distance restates the area card with more nuance

front: On the MCAT, what value of $g$ should you use, and who falls faster — heavy or light objects?
why: g = 10 advice plus all objects fall alike restates other cards in this deck

front: Projectile motion: what determines hang time?
why: Hang time set by the vertical component, t = 2 v0 sin(theta)/g; tested every year

front: Projectile range: formula, and which launch angle maximizes it?
why: Range formula with 45-degree maximum and complementary angles is tested every year

front: State the Big 5 kinematic equations and how to pick between them.
why: The Big 5 kinematic equations are the foundation of every kinematics calculation

front: Strobe images of a falling ball spaced farther apart each flash indicate {{c1::constant downward acceleration}}.
why: Strobe spacing as evidence of constant acceleration is a plausible passage figure question

front: Terminal velocity occurs when {{c1::drag equals weight}}, making acceleration {{c1::zero}}.
why: Terminal velocity when drag equals weight, a = 0, is tested on nearly every exam

front: The horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are linked only through {{c1::the time of flight}}.
why: Horizontal and vertical motions linked only by time; commonly needed setup step

front: The unit $m/s^2$ reads as {{c1::meters per second, per second}}.
why: Reading m/s^2 as meters per second per second is generic unit advice

front: The velocity of A relative to B equals {{c1::$v_A - v_B$}}.
why: Relative velocity v_A - v_B is a common vector question

front: Total stopping distance splits into a reaction part scaling with {{c1::$v$}} and a braking part scaling with {{c1::$v^2$}}.
why: Reaction distance scaling with v and braking with v^2; secondary proportional reasoning

front: Two cars travel at 60 and 40 km/h. What relative speed does each measure?
why: Two-car relative speed example restates the relative-velocity card

front: Two sprinters have identical average speed over 100 m but different acceleration profiles. What is equal on their v-t graphs?
why: Equal areas under v-t curves for equal displacement; secondary graph reasoning

front: Two velocity-time lines cross. Do the two objects meet at that instant?
why: Crossing v-t lines mean equal speeds not meeting; plausible but second-tier graph question

front: What implicit values do "dropped", "comes to rest", "at the peak", and "constant velocity" give you?
why: Implicit values from wording like dropped or at the peak are needed on most kinematics problems

front: What is the acceleration of a projectile at its highest point?
why: Acceleration g at the highest point restates the apex card in this deck

front: What is the FIRST step in any kinematics problem?
why: Generic first-step problem-solving advice

front: When are the standard kinematic equations valid at all?
why: Kinematic equations valid only for constant acceleration is a commonly tested condition

front: Which quantity is a vector?
why: Velocity as a vector restates the displacement/distance vector card

front: Why do a heavy and a light block slide down a frictionless incline together?
why: Mass independence on an incline supports the g sin(theta) card

front: Why is a projectile's path parabolic?
why: Why the path is parabolic is useful understanding but rarely the tested point

front: Why is instantaneous velocity a tangent slope while average velocity is a chord slope?
why: Tangent vs chord slope for instantaneous vs average velocity; supporting graph concept
